Bellingcat March Challenges

Background Check

Bellingcat Challenges March

Introduction

I completed the March challenges some time ago. It's so much faster to complete them than to write it all down. So, with some delay, here is how I solved everything:

Ship Happens

Initial analysis
Initial analysis: We see a picture of Peter in some kind of public place with a statue of a camel. The clothing and the flag in the background give strong Arab vibes. This narrows the list of places already significantly. We also know he was brought by ship, so the location must be at the ocean, or at least a river. It looks like a ship in the background, but this might be an ugly building too. He looks to be in some kind of airport-like structure.

Getting to the solution
After downloading the image, we find no metadata. No useful text is visible when zooming in, and I didn’t manage to translate the writings that are visible in the banner on the background.
Reverse-image searching this I found a link to website called “Cruise Critic”.

Here, someone reported a cruise journey that led through the same terminal. This journey was done with the MSC Euribia, and the Camel was standing in the Abu Dhabi Cruise terminal. When looking at images of the MSC Euribia, you can see that the pattern matches the background as seen in Peter’s image. Note the blue patterns on the ship matching.

Concluding, I'm confident to say that Peter was travelling on the MSC Euribia.

On the Right Track

Initial analysis
Peter is at a train station that is partially electrified. The place instantly reminded me of the Baltics and especially Latvia, where I've been many times. This is because of how the tracks look (not very well maintained), the soviet looking Water tower and the type of cars in the background.
The coat shows two flags, a Swedish one and an Austrian or Latvian one. This may be an extra hint that Peter is really present in Latvia.

Getting to the solution
Just because I wanted to be very sure, almost as to counter tunnel-vision, I looked up how electric railways look in Sweden. And they look better maintained, or at least, they do not have as much grass in between the tracks. So, Peter most likely is in the Baltics.

My first hunch was to use the Bellingcat OSM tool to find the location of Peter. As we can see that he is on a station, near a bus stop (visible behind the fence), and a water tower, I was expecting that it would not take very long to find the location. However, probably because of my own inexperience with the tool, I did not manage to find the location easily this way. So I changed tactics.

Life experience helps
I have been to Latvia many times. This helps. I happen to know that not all railways in Latvia are electrified. This is a good starting point to search.


As one can see in Figure 5, the amount of Latvian electrified railway is limited. That's where I decided for the next tactic: trace the railways using Google Maps satellite imagery and see whether I can find a station that matches the station where Peter is located. The station is picking up passengers (otherwise Peter wouldn't be there), it should have extra tracks for freight and there should be the water tower nearby.

I chose to start to search from Jelgava to Riga, because I know that Jelgava is a city that tourists might want to visit. No stations matched my search. Next, I chose to follow the tracks from Tukums to Riga (the most Western railway). The station called Sloka matched my search.

As you can see in figure 6, the water tower is visible and marked with red, the store is marked in dark blue, the bus stop is marked in yellow and the approximate location of Peter is marked in light-blue. In short; Peter is at the Sloka station, which is a neighborhood of Jurmala, Latvia.

Royal Company

I'll keep this description a bit shorter, because I found the location of Peter almost instantly this time.

We can see that Peter is in a European city, which I judged to be maybe German or Polish at first glance.

Zooming in on the image, the number-plate of the car on the right is visible. It says NEL 70798.

I quickly found that the only numberplate that fits the combination of 3 letters and then 5 digits is the Polish one. As can also be seen on Wikipedia, NEL corrolates to Ełk County. In turn, the city of Ełk is the only city in the county, making it our most likely candidate to have such an artwork.

Next, I went to Google Maps searched for statues in Ełk. Quickly, I found that the statue where Peter was located was named Rzeźby Królów Polskich and that it was located next to a street named Nadjeziorna.

No Room for Error

We see Peter reflected in a hotel room, while a European city is visible in the dark. Let's find the hotel.

Initial Analysis
The city in the background is European, judged by the layout and the cars visible. It's a Western or Northern European city probably, as the streets are very clean and everything is looking Modern. It actually reminded me of the Nordic countries, from my personal experience (I have been to Finland a lot, and it looks a bit like Finland).

Getting to the solution
First I checked the meta-data of the image, but nothing useful can be seen there. I looked for landmarks, but there were not many, except for the two very high chimneys in the distance. Too generic. Google Lens was not useful in this image, partly because of the way the reflection messes up the reverse-search and because of the lack of landmarks.

The sign with the arrow pointing to the right, visible in the left part of the provided image, looked like a good way to narrow down at least the country where Peter might be at. Traffic signs differ slightly from country to country, and the blue and white stripes, shape of the arrow, color of the sign and the white ring around the sign provide enough detail. Wikipedia has images of all the signs in the different EU countries, and this sign matched Sweden exactly.

I double checked by going around on streetview in Sweden, and this sign seems always to come with the blue bands, further solidifying the idea that Peter is in Sweden.

This helps a lot. Now, to find the location of Peter, I used a tactic which is probably not the most efficient. But it did work. I went around on Google maps, looking at the road layout, and tried to match it.

To increase the chances of a hit, I first narrowed down my search area even further. I figured that Peter would be in a big city, so a city with >100.000 residents. The most visited city in Sweden by tourists is Stockholm, so I decided to start there. Peter is in a relatively new neighborhood, not in the old center. But he probably wants to be close to the old city center, where the tourist attractions are.

My feeling was to center the center of Stockholm looking for newer neighborhoods, consisting of the modern blocky buildings that are visible in the image. Turns out, not many places are build like this, close to the center. But I did find

The area of Södra Hammarbyhamnen matched this description. Furthermore, there was a bit that matched the road layout, a you can see in Figure 13.

Not only does the road layout matches, the artwork visible in the background of Peter's photo is also marked on Google maps, and Streetview is also pretty conclusive.

Now we know the location, so we also know what hotel Peter stayed at: Motel L Hammarby Sjöstad.

Cold Case

March concluded with the most fun challenge, finding Peter's location based on a picture of a cold snack.

Initial Analysis
The ice-cream has Asian characters all over it, which I guessed were Korean (I think they look more blocky than Japanese or Chinese characters). It looked like Peter was in a train-station, metro-station, or possibly airport, because of the tiles and the lighting (spoiler, wrong assumption).

Getting to the solution
Again, no meta-data was present. Using Google Lens, I could translate part of the characters on the package of Ice-cream. Indeed, it is Korean, meaning that Peter is probably in South-Korea.

Google Lens did not provide any more useful data, such as locations etc. I looked up pictures of different kind of stations in Seoul, however, I concluded that stations don't use these tiles, and that it still would be like finding a needle in a haystack. I needed a different tactic.

Instead, I downloaded the provided image on my phone. Here, I altered the image using the "magic eraser" to remove the ice-cream, leaving me with an image that mostly resembles the floor underneath. It's not perfect, but good enough.

Reverse-search did work with this image. I found, after some scrolling, a result that looked very promising:

This street is in Seoul, Korea, and matches the tiles pretty well. Small colourful tiles, largely with a non-repeating pattern. However, the image (and the person that posted this) did not write exactly where this picture was taken. No stores are visible, for instance.

However, after searching for "colourful street seoul" on Google, it turns out that Hongdae Shopping Street is the most famous one in Seoul - it's a tourist attraction in itself.

To find out whether this is the right street, I went to Google Streetview. However, back when Google indexed this street into streetview, it looked very different from what it looks now. So I needed another way to "walk" down the street.

So I found a Youtube video of someone filming the experience of walking down Hongdae Shopping Street.

The video, showing the same location, does show what stores are nearby. I found one of these stores via Google Maps. From there, I found that a 7-Eleven is just around the corner. And just to confirm, the Video, at 0:42, shows that 7-Eleven. Roughly, assuming Peter and the man in the video walk about the same speed, that means that Peter took this picture roughly 25 seconds after leaving 7-Eleven. Explains why the ice-cream is still frozen!
